story: Petersburg starts drafting data center rules, a nine-month moratorium and Title 19 zoning, after a waterfront data center proposal tied to an idle 2-megawatt cannery transformer

claims.claim: The Petersburg Borough Assembly took up two data center items at its regular meeting on October 5th.
claims.verbatim: On the regular Assembly agenda today are two items regarding data centers.
claims.notes: Background (dated before the October 11th window), a same-day meeting preview by Taylor Heckart. 'Today' is the October 5th dateline. The October 16th KFSK follow-up reports the outcome of this meeting. The borough meeting portal was not reachable (petersburgak.gov returned HTTP 403), so no primary agenda or minutes were fetched.

claims.claim: The Assembly directed the Borough Manager and staff to draft an ordinance for a nine-month moratorium on certain data center projects.
claims.verbatim: Assembly members directed the Borough Manager and staff to draft an ordinance for a nine-month moratorium
claims.notes: In window. Olivia Rose, KFSK. The sentence goes on 'on certain data center projects.' Corroborated by the October 5th KFSK preview: 'Stanton Gregor is proposing a shorter, nine-month pause on permitting for data centers'. This is a direction to DRAFT and not an enacted moratorium. Phrase it as 'directed staff to draft'.

claims.claim: Vice Mayor Jeigh Stanton Gregor proposed the moratorium.
claims.verbatim: One proposes a temporary data center moratorium, recommended by Vice Mayor Jeigh Stanton Gregor.
claims.notes: Background date. Corroborated by the October 16th KFSK article: 'The Assembly unanimously approved Stanton Gregor's recommended moratorium.'

claims.claim: The proposed moratorium would restrict data centers that use on-site power generation.
claims.verbatim: restricting data centers from using on-site power generation
claims.notes: In window. This is a fragment of a longer sentence; the fetch tool returns excerpts only. The October 5th preview words it as a pause on data centers 'that either cannot operate' (on the grid, per the summary) 'or that don't use a closed-loop cooling system.'

claims.claim: The proposed moratorium would also cover data center facilities that don't use a closed-loop cooling system.
claims.verbatim: facilities that don’t use a closed-loop cooling system.
claims.notes: In window. The verbatim string keeps the source's curly apostrophe. The October 5th KFSK preview has the same phrase: 'or that don't use a closed-loop cooling system.'

claims.claim: Under the moratorium proposal, developers could still apply for a building permit if their project would be on Petersburg's grid.
claims.verbatim: Developers could still apply for a building permit if their project would be on Petersburg’s grid.
claims.notes: In window. This is central to the deck's thesis. The moratorium targets off-grid or on-site power and open-loop cooling, and grid-connected projects stay eligible to apply.

claims.claim: The Assembly approved Stanton Gregor's moratorium direction unanimously.
claims.verbatim: The Assembly unanimously approved Stanton Gregor’s recommended moratorium.
claims.notes: In window. What was approved is the direction to draft the moratorium ordinance, not a moratorium in force (see C11).

claims.claim: Assembly Member Jeff Meucci brought the second data center proposal.
claims.verbatim: The other proposal about data centers came from Assembly Member Jeff Meucci.
claims.notes: In window. Corroborated by the October 5th preview: 'Assembly member Jeff Meucci is also bringing forward a request regarding data centers.'

claims.claim: The Assembly directed the manager to draft changes to the borough's zoning code, Title 19, to regulate data centers.
claims.verbatim: Additionally, members directed the manager to draft changes to the borough’s zoning code (Title 19)
claims.notes: In window. The same article says the direction includes any necessary 'assistance from outside consultants'. The October 5th preview adds 'Petersburg's laws currently have no language about data centers.'

claims.claim: The Assembly approved Meucci's zoning proposal unanimously.
claims.verbatim: The Assembly approved Meucci’s proposal unanimously.
claims.notes: In window.

claims.claim: Both measures must return to the Assembly for consideration and public hearings before either can take effect.
claims.verbatim: consideration, and public hearings, before either measure can take effect.
claims.notes: In window. This is the end of a longer sentence. The deck must not say a moratorium is in effect. No KFSK report dated after October 16th was found on the KFSK data center tag page, and a Petersburg Pilot search found no data center story, so nothing confirms a first reading yet.

claims.claim: The moratorium as proposed would apply across the entire borough except the City of Kupreanof.
claims.verbatim: across the entire borough, except the City of Kupreanof.
claims.notes: In window. Fragment. The October 5th preview corroborates 'borough-wide moratorium'.

claims.claim: Petersburg Borough incorporated 3,829 square miles when it became a borough in 2013.
claims.verbatim: When Petersburg became a borough in 2013, it incorporated 3,829 square miles
claims.notes: In window article, background fact (2013). There is no second source. Use it for scale only, attributed to KFSK.

claims.claim: The September moratorium proposal had been limited to the borough's municipal service area, which ends roughly nine miles south of town.
claims.verbatim: it was limited to the Borough's municipal service area, which ends roughly nine miles south of town.
claims.notes: In window. This sentence is about the failed September proposal's scope. The scout's wider claim that 'zoning applies only within the service area' was NOT confirmed verbatim (see killed). The page says the borough began extending zoning regulations borough-wide earlier this year.

claims.claim: In September the Petersburg Planning Commission asked the Assembly for a year-long moratorium on data center applications or permits.
claims.verbatim: In September, the local Planning Commission asked the Assembly for a year-long moratorium on issuing applications or permits
claims.notes: In window. Corroborated by KFSK on September 28th: 'asked the Borough Assembly for a year-long freeze on issuing applications or permits for data centers.'

claims.claim: The Assembly considered the Planning Commission's moratorium request on September 21st.
claims.verbatim: The Petersburg Borough Assembly on Sept. 21 considered pursuing a temporary moratorium regarding data centers.
claims.notes: Background (before the window). Olivia Rose, KFSK.

claims.claim: The Assembly's vote on the year-long moratorium request ended in a 3 to 3 tie, so it failed.
claims.verbatim: landing in a tie 3–3 vote after discussing it for 30 minutes.
claims.notes: Background date. CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF: this was an ASSEMBLY vote on the Planning Commission's recommendation, not a Planning Commission vote. The verbatim string keeps the source's en dash; render the figure as '3 to 3' in deck copy. Corroborated by KFSK on October 16th: 'but the vote failed in a 3–3 stalemate.' The same September 28th article reports Assembly Member James Valentine 'was not present.'

claims.claim: Stanton Gregor called the possibility of a data center running on diesel-generated power and bypassing the grid probably far-fetched but worth noting.
claims.verbatim: He called that possibility “probably far-fetched,” but worth noting.
claims.notes: In window. Only 'probably far-fetched' is his direct quote; the rest of the sentence is the reporter's paraphrase. The preceding text refers to 'a data center that runs on diesel-generated power'. If quoted, quote only those three words.

claims.claim: Assembly Member Bob Martin said of the data center ordinance that 'we got to get something on the books.'
claims.verbatim: but we got to get something on the books,” Martin said.
claims.notes: In window. Verbatim tail of Martin's quote. The same article says 'Assembly Member Bob Martin called getting the ordinance process on data centers going, "a good idea."' Martin voted against the September moratorium, per KFSK on September 28th.

claims.claim: Petersburg's municipal utility department is drafting an ordinance to regulate large power users such as data centers.
claims.verbatim: The municipal utility department is drafting an ordinance for regulating large power users, such as data centers.
claims.notes: Background date. The October 16th article echoes it: 'there are regulations already being developed for large power users, plus existing utility safeguards'. KFSK reports Utility Director Steve Harbour told the Petersburg Pilot the ordinance is 'nearly done' (second-hand, not used).

claims.claim: Greensparc is a Silicon Valley-based company that builds small-scale data center facilities in communities with unused, stranded power and renewable energy.
claims.verbatim: building its small-scale facilities in communities with things like unutilized, stranded power and renewable energy.
claims.notes: Background (May 1st). The same article says 'The proposed private project is between the Silicon Valley-based company Greensparc' and that founder and CEO Sam Enoka 'is from Alaska's interior.' It describes the company's own self-description.

claims.claim: Developer Andrew Mazzella owns the defunct Ocean Beauty Seafoods property on Petersburg's downtown waterfront.
claims.verbatim: the developer who owns the defunct Ocean Beauty Seafoods property on the downtown waterfront.
claims.notes: Background. KFSK on September 28th refers to the developer as Mazzella Alaska, with Company President Tara Favilla.

claims.claim: Mazzella bought the former Ocean Beauty properties in 2024.
claims.verbatim: Mazzella bought the former Ocean Beauty properties on Petersburg’s downtown waterfront in 2024.
claims.notes: Background.

claims.claim: Mazzella also owns the 2-megawatt transformer that powered the cannery.
claims.verbatim: Mazzella also owns the 2-megawatt transformer that powered the cannery before the plant ceased operations in 2016.
claims.notes: Background. The scout's '1.5 MW in a borough FAQ' was not found on any fetched page (killed). Use 2 megawatts.

claims.claim: The Ocean Beauty cannery ceased operations in 2016.
claims.verbatim: Mazzella also owns the 2-megawatt transformer that powered the cannery before the plant ceased operations in 2016.
claims.notes: Background. Same sentence as C24.

claims.claim: Mazzella is penalized thousands of dollars a month by the borough utility department for not using the transformer's power.
claims.verbatim: Mazzella is penalized thousands of dollars by the local Borough’s utility department each month
claims.notes: Background. NEEDS SOFTENING: this is Mazzella's own account and the utility has not confirmed it. Write 'Mazzella says he pays' or 'according to Mazzella'. His quote: 'we're just bleeding money if we don't use the power.'

claims.claim: Petersburg runs on hydropower.
claims.verbatim: Petersburg runs on hydropower.
claims.notes: Background. The same article says diesel generators back up the system during high demand, outages, or the regional supplier's annual maintenance shutdown. 'Mainly hydropower' is the safest phrasing.

claims.claim: Petersburg has its own hydro plant south of town but buys most of its power from the Southeast Alaska Power Agency.
claims.verbatim: but buys most of it from Southeast Alaska Power Agency, a regional supplier that sends power to Petersburg
claims.notes: Background. The preceding clause is verbatim 'It has its own plant south of town,'.

claims.claim: The Southeast Alaska Power Agency supplies power to Petersburg, Wrangell and Ketchikan.
claims.verbatim: a regional supplier that sends power to Petersburg, Wrangell and Ketchikan.
claims.notes: Background. Widely known regional fact, but SEAPA's own site was not fetched.

claims.claim: Petersburg's utility projected a 5 percent rate increase for 2028.
claims.verbatim: points to a 5% utility rate increase projected for the year of 2028.
claims.notes: Background. NEEDS SOFTENING: a projection from a utility chart cited by then-utility director Karl Hagerman (described as 'outgoing'; KFSK on September 28th names Steve Harbour as utility director). Write 'projected'. The chart itself was not seen.

claims.claim: The utility's chart showed the 2028 projected increase falling to 0 percent if a full 2 megawatts were sold to a data center.
claims.verbatim: The following chart shows that projection falls to 0%, factoring for selling a full 2-megawatts of power to a prospective data center.
claims.notes: Background. NEEDS SOFTENING: a modeled projection that assumes the FULL 2 MW is sold. SANITY CHECK: this single-year 2028 figure (5 to 0) sits beside a different multi-year figure in the same article (about 4 to about 2 percent a year, C33). They measure different things, so never merge them. The Greensparc deal later 'did not finalize' (C37).

claims.claim: Petersburg's utility department estimated the data center would generate 1 to 2 million dollars in revenue a year.
claims.verbatim: they estimate it’d generate $1–2 million in revenue each year by operating that privately owned transformer.
claims.notes: Background. This RESOLVES the scout's 'borough FAQ' figure: it appears in KFSK's own reporting, attributed to the utility department. The FAQ itself was never reached (petersburgak.gov returned HTTP 403). Attribute it to the utility department via KFSK, not to an FAQ. NEEDS SOFTENING: write 'estimated'. The verbatim keeps the source's en dash; render as '$1 million to $2 million' in copy.

claims.claim: Petersburg utility rates were projected to rise about 4 percent a year for several years, and the data center would lower that to about 2 percent.
claims.verbatim: are projected to increase annually by about 4% for the next several years.
claims.notes: Background. The second half is also verbatim on the page: 'the data center would lower that figure to about 2%.' This resolves the scout's '4 to 2 percent' FAQ figure via KFSK. NEEDS SOFTENING: a utility projection. KFSK also reports the department says any rate increases would not be caused by the data center. See the C31 sanity note.

claims.claim: The Greensparc proposal would use the former cannery's existing power service, and the utility said it had enough surplus power to support it.
claims.verbatim: The department assures that there is enough surplus power to support the data center operation,
claims.notes: Background. THESIS CHECK, quoted and not inferred. The same article says the project would 'use the former cannery's existing power infrastructure' (the transformer). KFSK on September 28th says the developer 'seeks to use the site's existing industrial-sized power feed.' No fetched page describes on-site generation for this project. The only mention is Becky Knight's question about a 'micro-grid' Greensparc 'may be considering' (C40). That is enough to say the proposal as reported would draw utility (mainly hydro) power through the existing service. It is NOT enough to say it is certain to, so hedge with 'as described to KFSK'. The utility also said diesel backup would run more often during outages and SEAPA maintenance, and that it would seek a written agreement so those costs don't fall on all ratepayers.

claims.claim: Greensparc describes its cooling as a closed-loop system that works like a car radiator.
claims.verbatim: It uses a closed-loop cooling system that works like a car radiator
claims.notes: Background. THESIS CHECK: the page also says 'the cooling loop is filled up once, the water takes in heat,'. NEEDS SOFTENING: this is the company's own description. Write 'Greensparc says'. Read with C04 to C06: as described, the project is grid-connected and closed-loop, the category the October 5th moratorium direction leaves eligible to apply. That last link is our inference and no fetched page states it. If used, frame it as a reading of the rules, not as a reported fact.

claims.claim: Greensparc CEO Sam Enoka said 'We're not drawing any water, and we're not putting any emissions out.'
claims.verbatim: We’re not drawing any water, and we’re not putting any emissions out, and we’re not putting any water out anywhere,
claims.notes: Background. Attributed to Enoka in the article's quote sequence. NEEDS SOFTENING: a company claim, so attribute it as 'Enoka said'. The same page also has the verbatim quote '"We're designed to plug-in and be an economic benefit for the utility and the rate payers in the community," Enoka said.' and 'Almost anywhere in the world is going to be easier than Alaska.'

claims.claim: The developer's business deal with Greensparc did not finalize, KFSK reported in late September.
claims.verbatim: Its private business deal with a Silicon Valley-based data center vendor, Greensparc, did not finalize.
claims.notes: Background date. CRITICAL for the deck: the Greensparc proposal must NOT be presented as live. Present it as the proposal that started the debate.

claims.claim: Mazzella Alaska confirmed it is still pursuing a small-scale data center aligned with its initially announced plan.
claims.verbatim: Mazzella Alaska confirmed it is still pursuing a small-scale data center aligned with the initially announced plan.
claims.notes: Background. The fetch tool reported this as a portion of a longer sentence. No new partner had been named. Company President Tara Favilla testified that 'This project has always been about putting an underutilized industrial property back into productive use.'

claims.claim: A data center was proposed in Wrangell as part of a larger port development.
claims.verbatim: Mazzella learned of a data center proposed in Wrangell as part of a greater port development
claims.notes: Background, single-sourced and second-hand. KFSK's summary says the port development is partly city-funded. No Wrangell source was fetched, and its current status is unknown. NEEDS SOFTENING: 'a data center was reportedly proposed in Wrangell'. Keep it as a passing mention only.

claims.claim: Petersburg resident Becky Knight urged the Assembly in a May 4th statement to enact a moratorium on cell towers and data centers until their impacts were analyzed.
claims.verbatim: A Borough moratorium should be enacted immediately to put a hold on such expansion until the impacts can be better and fully analyzed.
claims.source_outlet: Petersburg Borough Assembly meeting record (statement by Becky Knight)
claims.notes: Background. PDF text extracted by fetch_pdf_text.py (out/2026-11-01/pdf_text/petersburg_knight_statement_2026-05-04.txt); the verbatim is joined across PDF line breaks. This is the run's primary document for Candidate 1, and it names 'the proposed Greensparc data center'. It also says 'what are the impacts of a "micro-grid" as Greensparc may be considering?' That is a question, not evidence of on-site generation. It is one resident's view, so do not frame it as community consensus.

claims.claim: AEA estimates the Cook Inlet PowerLink transmission project will cost 413 million dollars.
claims.verbatim: CIPLink has an estimated cost of $413 million, of which $269 million has been secured to date,
claims.notes: In window. PDF text extracted by fetch_pdf_text.py; the URL was confirmed from AEA's Press Releases index. Corroborated by the AEA CIPLink project page: 'Estimated Cost: $413 Million'. NEEDS SOFTENING: 'estimated'.

claims.claim: AEA has secured 269 million dollars for Cook Inlet PowerLink.
claims.verbatim: CIPLink has an estimated cost of $413 million, of which $269 million has been secured to date,
claims.notes: In window. PDF text extracted by fetch_pdf_text.py.

claims.claim: About 142 million dollars of Cook Inlet PowerLink's cost is still to be identified.
claims.verbatim: leaving approximately $142 million still to be identified.
claims.notes: In window. PDF text extracted by fetch_pdf_text.py. SANITY CHECK: 413 minus 269 is 144, not 142. AEA says 'approximately', so the $2 million difference is AEA's rounding or an unexplained difference. Quote AEA's 'about $142 million' and don't present it as simple subtraction.

claims.claim: Cook Inlet PowerLink would include a submarine cable of about 40 miles between the Beluga area and the Kenai Peninsula.
claims.verbatim: The proposed project includes an approximately 40-mile submarine cable crossing between the Beluga area and the Kenai Peninsula, with converter stations in Beluga and Soldotna.
claims.notes: In window. PDF text extracted by fetch_pdf_text.py; the verbatim is joined across a line-break hyphen ('40-' / 'mile'). The release calls it Alaska's first HVDC transmission connection across Cook Inlet.

claims.claim: Cook Inlet PowerLink's initial 100 megawatt system would accommodate future expansion to 200 megawatts.
claims.verbatim: The initial 100-megawatt system would accommodate future expansion to 200 megawatts.
claims.notes: In window. PDF text extracted by fetch_pdf_text.py. For scale against Candidate 1, 100 MW is 50 times the Petersburg transformer's 2 MW.

claims.claim: Cook Inlet PowerLink targets a 2031 in-service date, with federally funded completion required by August 2032.
claims.verbatim: The project targets an in-service date of 2031, with federally funded project completion required by August 2032.
claims.notes: In window. PDF text extracted by fetch_pdf_text.py. NEEDS SOFTENING: 'targets'. AEA expects a competitive cable procurement in mid-2027, subject to funding.

claims.claim: Responses to AEA's submarine cable prequalification and request for information are due December 15th, after a virtual conference on November 4th.
claims.verbatim: A virtual pre-response conference is scheduled for Nov. 4, 2026, from 10:30 a.m. to noon, and responses are due Dec. 15, 2026, at 2 p.m. Alaska time.
claims.notes: In window. PDF text extracted by fetch_pdf_text.py.

claims.claim: AEA will receive about 32.8 million dollars through the Department of Energy's Grid Resilience State and Tribal Formula Grant Program.
claims.verbatim: The Alaska Energy Authority (AEA) will receive approximately $32.8 million in additional federal funding through the U.S. Department of Energy's Grid Resilience State and Tribal Formula Grant Program.
claims.notes: In window. PDF text extracted by fetch_pdf_text.py; the URL was confirmed from AEA's Press Releases index. It covers combined federal fiscal years 2025 and 2026, and is part of about $967 million DOE announced nationally.

claims.claim: Alaska's grid resilience allocation is the third largest among states, behind California and Texas.
claims.verbatim: Alaska's allocation is the third largest among states, behind California and Texas, and $12.8 million more than AEA anticipated.
claims.notes: In window. PDF text extracted by fetch_pdf_text.py. The ranking is AEA's claim, not checked against DOE's allocation table. Write 'according to AEA'.

claims.claim: The grid resilience allocation was 12.8 million dollars more than AEA anticipated.
claims.verbatim: Alaska's allocation is the third largest among states, behind California and Texas, and $12.8 million more than AEA anticipated.
claims.notes: In window. PDF text extracted by fetch_pdf_text.py. The implied anticipated figure is about $20 million.

claims.claim: Securing all of the grid resilience funds requires a 1.8 million dollar state match.
claims.verbatim: To secure all federal funds made available under this allocation, a $1.8 million state match is required.
claims.notes: In window. PDF text extracted by fetch_pdf_text.py.

claims.claim: The Department of Energy announced the Beluga to Healy transmission project would combine up to 150 million dollars in Defense Production Act funding with 268 million dollars in non-federal funding.
claims.verbatim: combines up to $150 million in DPA funding with $268 million in non-federal funding
claims.notes: Background (October 5th, before the window), and it overlaps deck No.80 of October 7th. DOE announced its 'intent to deploy' DPA funding, so NEEDS SOFTENING: 'up to' and 'intends to'. The same page has the verbatim 'Approximately 223 miles of new transmission line connecting Beluga and Healy will be built.'

claims.claim: EPA proposed on October 29th to approve Alaska's application for primary enforcement authority over Class VI carbon sequestration injection wells.
claims.verbatim: proposing to approve the State of Alaska's UIC program primacy application for Class VI injection wells
claims.notes: In window. FR document 2026-22085, docket EPA-HQ-OW-2026-4588; the publication date was confirmed via the federalregister.gov API. It is a proposal, not a final approval.

claims.claim: Approval would let the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission issue and enforce Class VI permits.
claims.value: Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission
claims.verbatim: Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission (AOGCC) to issue and enforce compliance with UIC Class VI permits.
claims.notes: In window. Approval would exclude wells in Indian country and in areas of exclusive federal jurisdiction (verbatim 'except those located within Indian country and those located within areas of exclusive Federal jurisdiction').

claims.claim: Comments on EPA's Alaska Class VI proposal must be received by December 14th.
claims.verbatim: Comments must be received on or before December 14, 2026.
claims.notes: In window. The API field comments_close_on also reads 2026-12-14. The document also says 'The EPA will hold one virtual public hearing during the comment period.' No hearing date is given.

claims.claim: Alaska applied to EPA for Class VI primacy on May 22nd.
claims.verbatim: On May 22, 2026, Alaska applied to the EPA under SDWA section 1422.
claims.notes: Background event cited in an in-window primary document.

stories_surviving: Petersburg writes data center rules (Southeast Alaska)
Railbelt transmission, the money still to find
EPA proposes Alaska Class VI primacy

killed.claim: Petersburg's Planning Commission voted 3 to 3 on a data center moratorium.
killed.why: Misattributed. KFSK (September 28th and October 16th) says the 3 to 3 tie was an ASSEMBLY vote on the Planning Commission's year-long recommendation. Replaced by C15 to C17.

killed.claim: A Petersburg Borough FAQ gives $1 to $2 million in annual revenue and rate increases cut from about 4 to about 2 percent.
killed.why: The FAQ was never reached (petersburgak.gov returned HTTP 403). The figures themselves ARE verified in KFSK's May 1st article, attributed to the utility department (C32, C33). Attribute them to the utility via KFSK, never to an FAQ.

killed.claim: The borough FAQ puts the transformer or data center load at 1.5 MW.
killed.why: Not found on any fetched page. Every fetched source says 2 megawatts.

killed.claim: Petersburg's zoning code applies only within the municipal service area.
killed.why: No verbatim support was captured. The only matching sentence describes the failed September moratorium's scope (C14). The article does say the borough is extending zoning borough-wide, but the full sentence was not captured.

killed.claim: The Greensparc data center would generate its own power on-site or run a micro-grid.
killed.why: Not supported. KFSK describes use of the existing transformer and utility surplus power. The only mention of a micro-grid is a resident's question in the Knight statement ('as Greensparc may be considering').

killed.claim: Petersburg's Greensparc data center project is moving ahead.
killed.why: Contradicted. KFSK reported on September 28th that the Greensparc deal 'did not finalize'. The developer is still pursuing a small-scale project with no named partner (C37, C38).

killed.claim: The Assembly held a first reading or hearing on the drafted moratorium or zoning ordinances after October 16th.
killed.why: No report found. The KFSK data center tag page's latest item is October 16th, and a Petersburg Pilot search returned no data center story.

killed.claim: Petersburg ordered a moratorium on data centers.
killed.why: False as phrased. The Assembly only directed staff to DRAFT an ordinance, which must return with public hearings before taking effect (C02, C11).

killed.claim: Enstar and MEA gas swap (Petroleum News, November 1st).
killed.why: Paywalled past the lede per the scout. Not fetched or verified.
